speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. Will he give us a progress report on discussions with the provinces of his government's austerity program? Can he say, in view of his declared intention to proceed with the medicare program next July 1, whether his government is prepared to give consideration to the situation of Canadians in those provinces that will be unable to proceed with the program next July 1 but who will be required to pay taxes to support the medicare program in other provinces?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON CURRENT MEETINGS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON CURRENT MEETINGS
speechtext: I have had a word with the Minister of Finance, who is chairman of the meeting. speechtext:
supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. which comply with the conditions set out in the legislation.

speechtext:

the light of the discussions which have taken place at the conference so far and some of the statements made by provincial representatives, would the Prime Minister not agree that it is now even more imperative to hold a conference with the provinces to establish priorities in connection with expenditures?

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext: May I call your attention, Mr. Speaker, and that of all members of this house to the presence in the Speaker's gallery of the distinguished minister of foreign affairs for Japan, Mr. Miki.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext:
Hear, hear.

On the orders of the day:

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext: I wish to address my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has any reply been sent to the rather stiff formal protest received from the Soviet government concerning the recent demonstration at the Soviet embassy in Ottawa?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext:
It is a fact that the government of the Soviet union did deliver a note to our ambassador in Moscow. I have not had the full opportunity to deal with this aide memoire with the care it deserves and will require, but it does contain one submission with which I wish to deal forthwith. The note contains these words:
There are all the reasons to state that the preparation and holding of this provocation went on with the obvious connivance of Canadian official authorities.
Mr. Speaker, the record is clear, and has been made clear to the Soviet ambassador in Ottawa, that in no way could it be suggested that Canadian authorities had in any way contributed to the incidents which took place at the Soviet embassy here a week ago. I made a statement in this house. That statement still stands. I expressed regret over the incident. We recognize our obligations under the convention regarding the protection of embassies in our capital, but there is not the slightest basis or justification for the allegation in the Soviet note.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext: As a supplementary question, in consequence of serious repercussions from the demonstration, are discussions still going on and can the minister report any progress as to steps that will prevent the recurrence of any such unfortunate incident?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker; we have made suggestions to the civic authorities of Ottawa.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext:
In
view of what the minister has said, is the government going to reject this note in so far as it alleges that these demonstrations were carried out with the obvious connivance of Canadian official authorities?
November 17, 1967

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext:
I have just
indicated that there is no basis for that statement and we will certainly reject that part of the note. The complete formal reply is a matter that I am now considering.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in his answer the Secretary of State for External Affairs said he had discussions with the police of Ottawa. As a supplementary question I ask what special plans are being made to protect consulates in other Canadian cities; and have discussions been initiated by the hon. gentleman's department toward that end?

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext: This matter has been anticipated and my information is that in Moscow, for instance, this has been done with the co-operation of the Soviet authorities.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext:
I said consulates in
Canadian cities that are affected.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF JAPANESE FOREIGN MINISTER
speechtext: Yes, that matter too is covered.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS IN WASHINGTON BETWEEN CANADIAN AND U.S. MINISTERS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS IN WASHINGTON BETWEEN CANADIAN AND U.S. MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, can the Minister of Transport report to the house on the conclusions of his talks held yesterday with his counterpart in Washington, the secretary of transport?

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS IN WASHINGTON BETWEEN CANADIAN AND U.S. MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there was a most encouraging and worth-while initial contact with Mr. Boyd, the secretary of transport in the United States. What I am now assured of is close personal working relationships with him and maximum co-operation between the two departments which are responsible for similar problems. I think this will guarantee that information from each country is made available to the other, and to the extent that independent research is done we will try to make it as complementary as possible to supplement the knowledge which is already available. I thought it was most worth-while, certainly from our standpoint; I am sure it will assist us in the important work of trying to take on the problem of auto travel safety, and it will also assist us so far as air safety regulations are concerned.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS IN WASHINGTON BETWEEN CANADIAN AND U.S. MINISTERS
speechtext: With the realization that the minister had only a certain amount of time to discuss these matters with his counterpart I should like to ask, as a supplementary question, whether the minister does not now feel, even after the brief discussion with the secretary, that it is more important than ever to develop Canadian standards.

Mr. Chairman, when this bill was being considered by the house during the second reading stage I suggested to the minister that it appeared from the wording of the bill, and more particularly from the minister's own remarks in support of it, that the primary purpose of the new department would be to serve the consumer interest. I said this was the primary reason for including under the jurisdiction of the new department a number of business regulatory functions. It appeared from the minister's remarks that the regulatory functions were included to help protect the consumers.
I therefore suggested to the house that in view of this fact it would be appropriate to change the name of the department so it would be called the department of consumer and corporate affairs instead of the department of corporate and consumer affairs. I said to the house that I would be prepared to propose an amendment to achieve this change so as to indicate to the public at large that the government, through the creation of this new department, will exercise its jurisdiction as fully as possible to serve the interests of the consumers of this country.
It is obvious that all of us are concerned about the rise in prices and inflationary pressures. Certainly, as the minister pointed out, he does not have within his immediate personal control the principal levers of fiscal and monetary policy. But I think it is clear that if the authority given to this new department is used creatively and constructively it can do much to ensure that the dollar earned by the citizens of this country will go as far as possible and that this department will have an effective role in dealing with the cost and price spiral which concerns every one of us today. I therefore move, seconded by the hon.

point is that the consumers of this country are beginning to demand that something be done under this bill. We hear frightening forecasts of what is to happen to the cost of living in the coming year. The Canadian Manufacturers Association says that the consumer price index, which in October of this year stood at 150.7, will go up to 154.8 by the middle of next year and that prices are to increase by an average of 5 per cent. Consumers are aware of what is happening, and they expect the minister to put real teeth into the bill.
Consumer protest associations from Montreal and Toronto have tried to approach the minister. I know the Montreal delegation was not successful in seeing him; I do not know what happened to the Toronto delegation. I do know that many other delegations from other parts of the country will come here and attempt to approach the minister.
In my remarks I shall talk about that part of the bill which affects the consumer. The other part also is important, but that will be dealt with by other members who will speak after I have spoken. We in this party have little quarrel with the provisions that are in this part of the bill. Our quarrel is that so much is left out. As a matter of fact, these things in the bill were recommended by the

consumer affairs committee. Our quarrel is with what is not in this bill.
[DOT] (12 noon)
What are the areas in which consumers need protection? Briefly, they are four-safety and quality, packaging and labelling, information and the cost of living. So far as the first two are concerned, they are looked after fairly well in the bill.
This is because the functions of consumer protection governing these matters are, with the exception of the food and drug directorate, being transferred to this department, and over the years, I must admit, an increasing amount of protection has been afforded by the government in this direction. I do not mean that consumers can afford to go to sleep. They cannot. But I do feel these matters are under control.
I wish to turn now to the other two areas, information and the cost of living. I wish to say plump and plain with regard to the cost of living that the consumers of this country are not going to get any special protection under this bill as now drafted unless real teeth, real muscle power which is not there now, can be put into it. I know that in Canada Month a few weeks ago the minister was warning us: "Until I have the muscle I don't want to talk too much; I am a weak department; I am the low minister on the totem pole." I suggest there are ways of being a higher minister on the totem pole and of getting more muscle into this bill. Before we have finished we in this party want to suggest ways and means of muscling the minister; I do not say "muzzling" the minister because we do not want to do that. But we want to muscle him to match his words when out on the hustings.
I do not want to see him fall into the category mentioned the other evening by the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas in her eloquent speech who referred to his performance as being all things to all men. I feel that strengthening his position would make it not all things to all women but to all consumers. Of course, a great many consumers are women. We know that according to a recent Gallup poll 45 per cent of the responses which came in put the cost of living as the most important aspect of consumer protection. In comparison, the other matters were very small indeed.
The minister has not been too forthcoming on the question of the cost of living. He was asked, again in Canada Month: "What does the N.D.P. want?" He said it wants consumer

programs with teeth; it wants a prices review board. Then we read: "But", says Turner with justifiable triumph, "where is the constitutional authority for that?"
The women who were here the other day said in their brief that if there is no possibility of getting federal action in co-operation with the provinces on this important matter of the cost of living, what in the name of time is the sense of setting up a federal consumer department? If the consumer department is not prepared to deal with the cost of living in any substantial way, what is the use of having such a department? I suggest to the minister that at this stage he must make a decision. Either he must put teeth into this department so it can deal with the cost of living or he must quit pretending that this is a consumer protection department in relation to the cost of living. I think these women were right when they said toward the conclusion of their brief:
In closing, the onus of proving that prices are exorbitant, and business practices in the retail food and retail drug companies corrupt, should not fall on the shoulders of the housewife. These essential items must be made available to all citizens at a price they can afford to pay.
This is exactly where these women are right, and before we are finished with this debate we shall make our proposal again to establish in this department a prices review board which will be able to take a long look at exorbitant prices, bring offences into the light of publicity and take whatever appropriate measures are required to hold the line in the essentials of life the consumer needs.
The whole committee was concerned about this question in various ways and I think it is time the minister grasped the nettle or told the consumers frankly: I shall not be able to do anything substantial about the cost of living. If he would come out frankly and tell them that, they would know they would have to turn some place else. The consumer is being conned if the bill is left as it is.
The minister is shaking his head and I know he wishes it were different, but changing the name of the department is not going to do anything to put real teeth in this bill.
Now I wish to turn to the other area which is not provided for adequately in the bill and that is the question of giving information. In the committee we were strongly impressed by the role which big advertising plays in raising the prices of goods to the consumer. This is what the committee said on this point:

The minister has also been showing concern about advertising. He has been talking about the need for protecting the consumer on various fronts. But I do not believe he can have expected the results he got the other day when the president of Canada's largest advertising company turned on him and bit him in a very sensitive spot indeed. The president of Canada's largest advertising agency has accused John Turner, Registrar General, of making confusing and contradictory attacks on advertising.

Labrador is part of Newfoundland. It was brought back to Canada by confederation and is one of the gifts Newfoundland gave Canada for which we were never properly thanked.
I am also happy, Mr. Chairman, that a man of energy, dynamism and ambition is to head this department. One of the problems in Newfoundland, if I may be provincial for a moment, is the very high cost of living which in turn is affected by freight rates. I make a strong distinction between cost of living and quality of life. I think we have the quality of life, but the cost of living seems to be just too much.
It might be pertinent here to recall the opinions offered by the Newfoundland royal commission on transportation, whose report was presented about a year and a half ago.
November 17. 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs In one section they pointed out that with the advent of confederation Newfoundland, which once dealt with England and the United States, became a captive market for Canada. In passing, Mr. Chairman, may I mention the fact that if you think of Newfoundland as a separate country and not as a province of Canada, Newfoundland would be Canada's third best customer. Only the United States and Great Britain buy more from Canada than does the province I represent.
Confederation also gave the province a freight rates structure not related to mileage or the cost of the services performed. This structure, said the report, was predicated upon the constitutional advantage created by confederation in favour of the mainland maritimes region, and it also provided a system tied to social need rather than economic reality. The effect on transport between Newfoundland and mainland Canada was serious. It gradually resulted in the elimination of most of the traditional water carriers who could not compete with the railway rates. It has been noted through the years how the C.N.R. reduced its rates in summer when there was direct shipping from Montreal and then raised them in winter when the St. Lawrence closed.
The report of the MacPherson federal royal commission on transportation recommended that the mainland maritime structure be altered by imposing rates related to the cost of operation. But MacPherson made special recommendations that the Newfoundland structure remain intact. I hope this will be the case.
This new department is concerned with both corporate and consumer affairs. The inclusion of the term "corporate" in its title should not, however, mislead the public into believing that the protection of the consumer interest will be a subordinate consideration. The department will in fact be heavily consumer oriented. The relationship between the corporate function and the consumer is obvious because the two are closely interrelated.
Let me try to show, Mr. Chairman, one or two ways in which the new department will have the power to act, and under this minister I know the power will be used, with discretion of course and always with justice.
Many of the recommendations of the joint committee on consumer credit and the cost of living relate to fields which fall within provincial jurisdiction. I am happy to hear that the minister has announced his intention of visiting all provincial capitals to discuss with

the provincial authorities a number of pressing consumer problems, along with finding possible solutions to them. It is the hope of the minister, and it is certainly my hope, that this will facilitate his being in a position to ensure that consumer protection is effectively co-ordinated throughout Canada.
One of the most important areas which now need federal-provincial co-operation, in my opinion-indeed, very close co-operation is required-is the acute problem of consumer credit. I should like to deal briefly with the specific subject matter of the problems confronting consumers in relation to credit. The five main problems in this regard, as I see them, are as follows. First of all, there is inadequate knowledge of the cost of credit from various institutions. Second, there is the high cost of credit. Third, there are unfair clauses in conditional sales contracts. Fourth, there is unwise use of credit. Fifth, there is the problem of the refunding of credit cost on prepayment of debt.
How are these problems to be dealt with? Dealing first with disclosure requirements, many provinces-I think most of them-have legislation requiring disclosure of credit costs in prescribed ways, including disclosure of credit costs on revolving charge accounts. The Bank Act and regulations thereunder now require disclosure by the banks of the cost of credit. The provinces and the federal government have co-operated in efforts to make this legislation uniform so that more meaningful comparisons may be made by credit users. The new department will seek to ensure that this co-operation is strengthened and the activity intensified.
The second problem I mentioned is the high cost of credit. Only under the Bank Act, the Small Loans Act, and certain provisions of the Quebec civil code are there limits put on credit costs. In other cases creditors are free to set the cost of credit at a rate which is subject to negotiation. A borrower who is a good credit risk, in comparison with a poor credit risk, will receive a much more favourable rate. One justification for this is that the cost to the lender of administering the loan to the good credit risk may be considerably lower t han the cost that may be incurred in administering loans to poor risk borrowers.
Several of the provinces now have unconscionable transactions relief legislation under which relief may be sought from excessively high interest rates. The new department, as I have already mentioned,
November 17, 1967

will be seeking to augment this protection through action under the Small Loans Act.
The third problem I referred to concerns unfair clauses in contracts. In almost all conditional sales contracts to be assigned by the original vendor to a finance company, there are the following clauses. For example, there is a clause which provides in effect that the goods are not covered by any warranty. Second, there is a so-called cut-off clause which provides that the finance company is not to be affected by equities between the seller and buyer. Third, the buyer is required to sign a promissory note for the amount due under the agreement, and this is a separate, absolute unconditional obligation to pay the purchase price and carrying charges.
I believe clauses of this type should be outlawed. Without these special clauses the law would impose an obligation on the seller to give reasonable satisfaction and, if he failed to do so, the buyer would not have to pay. With these clauses, however, the buyer's obligation to pay is absolute and unconditional and the seller is relieved of the obligation even to supply goods of adequate quality. There is no legislation which prevents the inclusion of these clauses in conditional sales contracts. At present, as we know, it is a case of the buyer beware. The new department, through liaison with the provinces, will seek to remedy this deficiency.
The fourth main problem has to do with the unwise use of credit. A by-product that can be expected as a result of the disclosure legislation is a wiser use of credit. People who are aware of the cost of borrowing may think twice and may borrow up to the limit set by their income rather than beyond and sometimes, to my knowledge, far beyond. I am told that in metropolitan Toronto there is a credit counselling service which is sponsored by the federal government, the provincial government and through private donations. Generally speaking, however, debt counselling is done by lending agencies which are not entirely disinterested in this matter. There is no doubt that the consumer interest can be afforded greater protection in this area through, among other things, consumer education, a matter which will be receiving high priority in the new department.
The fifth point is in respect of the refund of credit costs on prepayment of debts. It has been the common practice in respect of prepayment of debts, where this is permitted

Corporate and Consumer Affairs by the contract, to reimburse the borrower somewhat less than what he would consider to be a fair proportion and, in some cases, a great deal less. Some of the disclosure legislation which is now in effect requires disclosure of prepayment refund calculations at the time the contract is made. This, undoubtedly, is another field in which greater liaison between the provincial and federal authorities could serve to enhance further the protection of the public interest. The interest of the consumer is and will continue to be the main concern of the minister and the new department. Indeed, it will be the continuing concern of all thinking Canadians, including the representative of St. John's East in Newfoundland.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like my first words to be those of congratulation to the new minister. I wish him well in his position in which he has a very great responsibility to the consumers of this country. We know he is being groomed as the whitehaired boy for the Liberal leadership. I believe all of us would suggest that his prospects in this regard are tied in with the success he may have in administering this department and with the satisfaction the consumers of Canada will derive from his ministry.
There is reason for disappointment in respect of this legislation. As my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, pointed out, it is not so much what the bill says that is important but rather what the bill has omitted, namely, the teeth necessary to make this legislation effective.
The committee on consumer credit probably was one of the outstanding committees which has been set up by this House of Commons in a long time. Other committees have done effective work, but I like to think that this committee did a great job. I should like to congratulate the joint chairmen and all the members of the committee from all parties for the good work done by the special joint committee on consumer credit. The report of the committee containing its recommendations was hardly a radical document. It was valuable, however, in terms of establishing the idea that from now on the interests of the consumer would have to be a concern of the government. I regret that the government did not see fit to accept the recommendation of the committee that there should be a department of consumer affairs. Instead, the government has brought extraneous matters into this department.
4402	COMMONS DEBATES	November 17. 19S7
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
The work of the committee has been very valuable. A great body of information and knowledge was accumulated. Considerable research was done even though the staff was limited. Many misconceptions were cleared away and we were given an opportunity to see the problem more clearly and focus our attention on the real difficulties which are before us. The main point that was established was that business, labour and any other group in society would have to justify their behaviour to the consumers. No one was exempt. This point was made at the very first meeting of the committee when a witness expressed a wish that his evidence be given in camera. At that point the members of the committee decided that the information should be made public and that nothing should be withheld from the public. I believe this was an intelligent and wise decision. I think it is one which the public will applaud.
Publicity was provided concerning the work being done by the members of the committee. This I believe was an aid to the consumers. Some firms suffered as a result of the evidence which was given before the committee; they suffered as they deserved to suffer. Some firms were assisted considerably because the evidence given before the committee established that what they were doing was in the public interest and that their services were superior to those of others. I am convinced that during the period the meetings were being held the fact that the committee was in existence had the effect of restraining prices which might have risen more rapidly than they did. I believe that during that time everyone was looking over his shoulder and wondering to himself what would happen if a price increase were put through and he had to appear before the committee to justify it. These people probably were asking themselves: What would we have to say for ourselves? The representatives of some of the companies have already indicated that this in effect is what happened, that is, that during the course of those hearings prices were restrained.
I regret that this committee has not been reconvened. I think there is a great deal of valuable work which it could be doing. I hope that during the course of this debate the minister will find an opportunity to assure us that he intends to have the committee reconvened as soon as possible so that it can continue some of this work. We were unable, for instance, to look into the matter of automobile prices. The United Automobile Workers wrote the committee requesting that
[Mr. Saltsman.l
an investigation be made into the high price of automobiles in this country. Because of the other work being done by members of the committee at the time, that investigation was not held. I believe it should be held. There are good reasons for looking into the pricing practices of the automobile companies in this country.
The result of the work of the committee really was that the minister was provided with the shape and outline of a department of consumer affairs with a prices review board. This is the work the members of the committee were doing. They were reviewing prices and practices and, because the work was so valuable and constructive, the minister should seriously consider continuing a program of this kind on a permanent longterm basis by means of a committee or board composed of qualified professionals. I would not want that remark to be interpretated as meaning that we did not have qualified people. Some first class people assisted the committee and I should like to express my appreciation to the staff assigned to help, particularly Dr. Warren James who did an outstanding job on behalf of this group.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
We did not have enough people to do the work we set out to do. The committee meetings were very instructive in the early days when we were somewhat amateurish. Most of us came to the committee without any experience in these fields and it was difficult to come to grips with the complicated problems before us. However, as the meetings progressed the committee members became more astute in their questioning and more knowledgeable about these problems. I think this supports the need for more expertise and continuing examination of prices and practices in this country.
The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace played a very important role on that committee. He was one of the excellent members there and I recall some of his questions which came to grips with the suggestion of a prices review board. He was very sympathetic to the idea although, as he pointed out, he wanted some evidence that such a review board would produce the desired effect. I should like to quote some of the questions he posed at that time. There seems to be a gremlin around here who is walking away with the significant pieces of evidence I had. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace
November 17, 1967

in questioning Professor Neufeld is reported at page 124 as follows:
A way should be found to bring public opinion closer to the price-setting practices of all industry. I think you made the comment at that time, "but not this kind of a committee"?
Mr. Neufeld then said "no". Then Mr. Neufeld went on to say:
-I think as I mentioned before, this is an area in which one has to learn as one goes on. My hope would be, perhaps it is a futile one, that the justification in the first instance would be before public opinion. If the public has the information, and if it is known that the major price increases and wage increases must be justified on rational economic grounds then in this way it might be that public opinion will have a greater impact on these prices. That is where I would start to try to bring public opinion to bear on the price setting and wage setting mechanism-
A board would do exactly that because it would operate like the committee and would focus attention on price changes taking place in our society. It would ask for justification for these price changes and thereby provide the government with an opportunity to take action should it find the changes are not justified.
When a member of this party refers to the suggestion of a prices review board, almost invariably somebody asks about wages and whether we should not also look at them. I think we must look at everything, and I do not think the wage earner would be the slightest bit afraid to come before a review board to justify his behaviour. In fact wage earners do this every day of the week through collective bargaining. They must justify their demands, and they do so. It is interesting to note that this position was supported by the vice president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Dodge.
The minister will have to find new ways of tackling these problems on behalf of the consumers of this country. He should not be constrained by the need to walk on both sides of the fence. I do not know how the minister feels about this limitation on his authority but I would think it is very restrictive.
It has been pointed out that difficulties in respect of consumer and corporate affairs have some things in common. One could say that consumer affairs are related to almost everything else in our economic set-up, but that is not the point. What we must understand is that there is a branch of government for almost every interest in this country and sometimes branches for sectional interests. These interests must be reconciled and only
Corporate and Consumer Affairs one minister with undivided loyalty can speak on behalf of these interests. It is not the minister's job to balance interests between consumers and corporations. It is the minister's job, on behalf of the consumer only, to argue with the other ministers in the government in order to resolve these problems in cabinet, not in his own mind. Let us not make a Pooh-Bah of this minister, a high executioner on the one hand and a chancellor of the exchequer on the other. This would be an impossible task and one which would not do him credit. Nor could he do justice to the responsibility facing him today.
The minister will also have to be a bit of a radical. He will have to consider government intervention in economic affairs. The old method of leaving the market to itself will not help to solve the consumer problems which have developed for that very reason. Markets operating on their own have in many cases conspired in some way against the consumer's best interest. The minister must look not only with the eyes of the consumer but must rid himself of any dogma he may have. Many different types of economic ideas will be necessary, some coming from the socialist arsenal and others resulting from the valuable experience of free enterprise. The minister should not hesitate to take advantage of either in the interest of the consumer; otherwise he will do a disservice to those he is attempting to help.
Experience in Canada has indicated how important government intervention can be. This nation was built by government intervention in the economy and it is becoming increasingly obvious that many problems can be solved only through government participation. This fact is accepted today by all but a few die-hards. We have accepted what we call free enterprise for a long time and the results have not been as valuable as they might have been. It has often led to high costs, inefficiency and waste instead of productivity.
The minister must consider how to change the direction of market forces and how to direct competition into more meaningful channels in order to achieve lower prices. Competition may not always be necessary. Canadians will have to accept concentration and co-operation in some cases as the most effective way of lowering prices. The real issue in a matter of this type will not be the question of size or concentration but whether that concentration or size will be in the interests of the Canadian people, particularly the
consumer.
November 17, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Through our present combines legislation we have attempted to control the size of market power, but this has become a dead letter. It has completely failed its purpose and has not stopped harmful collusion. It has, on the other hand, prevented Canadian business and consumers alike from coming to grips with the real problem in respect of lower prices of goods and services. It is time the government faced up to the fact that our combines legislation does not serve the purpose for which it was intended and that we will have to find a better way of stimulating the economy and protecting the public interest than now exists. There are better ways. There are two general approaches that could be taken to this problem. One would be to pass more legislation setting up a larger organization for the detailed examination of business activity, to look over the shoulders of everything that is being done. The other way is for the government itself to provide some competition.
There are many things we could do. In consultation with industry we could determine those items of general use for which the Canadian market is big enough to provide maximum efficiency of scale. We could encourage manufacturers in Canada to reduce the variety of their products and go in for longer runs. Our productivity lags far behind what it should be. It lags far behind because of the splintered nature of our economy. Despite a far higher level of capital investment in our secondary industry, we are considerably less productive than those with lower capital investment.
A great deal has to be done in this area. We will have to encourage manufacturers in Canada to reduce the variety of their products and go in for longer runs, as I have already said. They may have to co-operate with each other. Immediately the suggestion of collusion arises and the question is asked: How do you protect the public interest in this case? I think a good case might be made to show that some of our firms must be larger. Then the question will be asked: How will the public interest be protected under these circumstances? I suggest to the minister that he has all the means at his disposal for solving this problem. He has at his disposal means far more effective than the combines legislation to protect the public interest, if only he is willing to use them. In respect of those products which are subject to international competition, I do not think there need be a great fear of abuse. I believe that tariff

legislation would protect the consumer in cases of this type while allowing our own manufacturers to reach efficient size and scale.
There are other measures that could be taken. Changes in the patent laws of this country would have a most salutary effect in protecting consumers. It would have a far better effect than the phony combines legislation that really does not work very effectively. For those industries that are not constrained by foreign pressures the minister will have to find new approaches. One of these new approaches, I suggest, is government competition. If competition is the answer in industry and that competition is not forthcoming from the private sector, I suggest it is time the government itself became a competitor in the economy in order to achieve the price reductions and provide the services needed by the consumer.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I do not think any of these decisions can be made unless the minister establishes a prices review board -perhaps it should be called a prices and practices review board-which would examine not only pricing but also the approaches being taken in the market itself. Such a board could examine the price changes that are introduced and decide how effectively measures are working to ensure that the lowest prices prevail. Under some circumstances it may even be necessary that some prices in this country be controlled. But that is a decision which could be made only after a thorough examination of an industry's pricing structure.

I recognize the difficulty the hon. member raises in any question of prices. I think we need at this stage a board to examine the price changes that are taking place and then make recommendations to the government for corrective action. I do not think such a board would have all the powers necessary to achieve adequate price control under some circumstances, but on the
November 17, 1967

basis of the board's examination of the situation it could report to the government. One of its recommendations might be for a tariff change, another might be for a patent change. Another recommendation might be that the federal government seek agreement with the provinces on controlling the price of certain items. There are constitutional problems, but I do not think they are insurmountable.
The point is that the government is not in a position even to know what the problem is until such a board is established to examine the changes and practices that are taking place in our society. Then action would become the responsibility of the government and not of the board. Only the government could have this responsibility. The board would indicate the direction and the kind of action that needed to be taken.
We have had today a discussion of advertising. I know there is some disagreement about what is good and what is bad advertising. I think all of us agree that the advertising being carried on at the present time is away beyond what is really necessary to move goods and services and inform the consumer. Even the advertisers themselves would in their lucid moments agree with this.
The question then resolves itself into the following: How do you sort out the good from the bad, rather than deciding whether all advertising is bad or good? The minister faces a very profound challenge in this problem. I am pleased to see that the minister is aware of the problem. I do not think the problem has been solved in any significant way by anyone in North America. This may be one of the most serious challenges facing the minister. I should like to quote from a newspaper article to remind the minister of his awareness of the problem. Referring to the minister, an article which appeared in the Regina Leader Post of September 22, 1967, says in part:
The minister said that Canadians spent 21 times as much last year on advertising as on higher education, and in the U.S. it has been found by the courts that huge corporations can approach monopolistic power by the weight of their advertising.
That is a good start. The minister is aware of the problem. Now that he has stated the problem and has noted the waste and the fantastic, incredible difference in the amount of money spent on advertising compared with that spent on higher education, he must do something about it. This is a real challenge and we will be waiting to see what sort of programs the minister develops. I point
Corporate and Consumer Affairs out to the minister that he will not be courting popularity in some circles, but the people will have reason to be grateful for changes that are made which reduce what is a social waste in this area at a time when we need whatever resources we can command for useful and valuable purposes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the future of the free market depends, I believe, on its ability to provide for the needs of all Canadians. I believe it to be the role of government to ensure that the system works to this end. This is not a new idea. In our country a large influence in this direction is the philosophy of Keynes, who in the thirties took this view after having the advantage of training by two great economic giants, Marshall and Pigou.
Keynes was always prepared to adjust his theories to the changing shape of the outside world. He felt that private enterprise and government were two powerful partners for growth. He believed society was made for man, and he favoured the role of the state in the mitigation of economic adversity wherever it appeared, always with the purpose of preserving and enlarging freedom. The bill introduced by the minister, a young, dynamic
November 17, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs and highly educated member of the House of Commons, I think approaches this interesting economic problem in response to the emergencies that we face in Canada arising from a particularly affluent society.
It might be worth while for us to review what it is that we collectively have accepted as our economic goals, objectives that will not be disputed by any member of the house. In 1963 the Economic Council of Canada was created by an act of parliament and established specific goals. Let us ponder them carefully. Full employment; a high rate of economic growth; reasonable stability of prices; a viable balance of payments; an equitable distribution of rising incomes. In short, Mr. Chairman, an optimum economic balance. John Deutsch has been one of the great apostles of this kind of economic balance throughout his years of service to Canada in various capacities. I congratulate the minister on bringing in a bill which I believe both in its style and its content does preserve something of balance.
Professor Galbraith, who is newsworthy as well as very highly respected as an economist, specifically developed the theory of social balance. He followed other theorists such as R. H. Tawney, who in his famous text "Equality" writes:
-slowly and reluctantly, amid prophecies of moral degeneration and economic disaster, society began to make collective provision for needs which no ordinary individual, even if he works overtime all his life, can provide himself.
This is written by one of the champions of freedom who believes freedom can in fact be enlarged by wise governmental action which is complementary to that great engine of progress, private enterprise.
I have been looking at price trends in Canada and at some of the statistics relating to our problems associated with rising prices. To understand our situation in Canada we must always make comparisons with other countries. The fact is that in recent years the Canadian experience relatively has been highly favourable.
I have been studying the change in the cost of living that has occurred in 27 countries between 1958 and November, 1966. The percentage change has universally been that of increase; in other words, the change has tended toward inflation. The United States has the lowest record of inflation of all these countries with only 14 per cent. Canada is second lowest with 16 per cent. The third lowest of these 27 countries is Australia.

However, sir, I would point out that a country as prosperous as Germany has had an increase of 22 per cent since 1958. Switzerland, which we regard as one of the most stable of world economies, has had a 26 per cent increase. The United Kingdom, with several changes in government and a willingness on the part of government to be radical and to innovate, shows an increase of 27 per cent. There are no less than 11 important countries of the world, including Italy, France, Japan, Israel and Yugoslavia, which have had increases ranging from 34 per cent up to 167 per cent. So, Mr. Chairman, by all objective standards Canada's record has been quite remarkable. Let us bear in mind that we are, after all, a nation of only 20 million people trading in this large international complex of nations and influenced, therefore, by the inflationary tendencies prevailing in all parts of the world.
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I am satisfied that we must judge any economic proposal we bring into this house on the basis of what effect that proposal may be likely to have on the optimum allocation of resources as well as on patterns of saving and investment. If anyone laughs at this as academic, I would argue that in the middle and long run these are in fact the factors that are going to determine the consumption of Canadians and the cost of goods that they will be able to enjoy.
e (2:40 p.m.)
Sir, social imbalance, according to Galbraith in "The Affluent Society", is the natural offspring of persistent inflation. Inflation by its nature strikes different individuals and groups with highly discriminatory effects. The most nearly unrelieved victims, apart from those living on pensions or other fixed provisions for personal security, are those who work for the state. He points out in his text how parts of the private sector can deal with inflation. Private firms can adjust to inflation by increasing prices. Management and labour, by their organization, can protect themselves by increasing prices and wages but others are grievously injured. That is why this bill, that permits the minister to initiate and undertake programs designed to promote the interest of Canadian consumers and to co-ordinate programs, to co-operate with provincial governments-a basic necessity of this department-as well as to undertake research into matters affecting costs, sound balance has been reached in the unremitting struggle against higher prices.
November 17, 1967	COMMONS
W. A. Preshing of the University of Alberta, said about the Canadian consumer:
While installed horsepower and output per production worker almost doubled in the two decades from 1920 to 1940, average hourly wages increased by one-third. This rising productivity passing on to the same number of production workers with only limited increases in income caused prices to fall. Business, producing the same products, was forced to lower selling prices, with consequent under consumption contributing to the stagnation of the economy.
That condition also contributed to growing unemployment. Preshing says that the second world war, with its emphasis on research, brought quite a change not only by bringing about changes in old products but by assisting in the creation of new products.
A new state of affairs was therefore brought into being and this has been described in the writings of J. A. Schumpeter. New products were produced and we are now enjoying them every day. I continue to quote from W. A. Preshing:
The immediate post-war period saw a reversal of the economic conditions outlined above. Incomes, rising faster than productivity, created more discretionary income and helped emphasize the importance of marketing innovation.
An hon. member who preceded me spoke a few minutes ago about the importance of having teeth in the bill. I cannot put my hands on the study but I have read an analysis of the ineffective results gained heretofore by placing too great a reliance on the Criminal Code to contain, control and direct economic activity. I have had some modest experience in this area as a lawyer and I have seen how inequitably in certain instances is the application of the code. We know that the Department of Justice may use sections 303, 304, 306, 323, 324, 349, 350, 351 and 354. From time to time the department prosecutes under those sections.
The code does not afford, I believe, much protection to the consumer. Greater protection lies in multilateral trade. May I quote the basic economic argument enunciated recently by Harry G. Johnson before he left for his chair at the London School of Economics. He said at a convocation in Kingston:
The problem that will face Canadian policymakers will be, how to safeguard as much of Canada's trading interests-and through them her prosperity-as can be preserved in a fragmenting international economy.
He speaks of how we are to obtain our greatest material rewards and says:
It will be of vital importance to Canada for the policy-makers' logical heads to rule their emotional hearts, and for them to stick to the principle that Canada's economic interests lie in freer trade and larger markets.
DEBATES	4407
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
Let us never forget in the course of our discussion on prices, Canada's great economic accomplishments in the last few years, compared with the accomplishments of other advanced countries of the world.
Jim MacDonald, executive secretary of the National Labour Co-operative Committee, says in Canadian Labour of October, 1963, that $200,000 is the approximate amount of money which the average Canadian worker will earn and spend in his lifetime. This reminds me of something written recently by Charles Graham entitled, "The Capricious Consumer". He refers to the sombre conclusions of Thorstein Veblen who was writing in times of unemployment and great economic inequality. In many ways the problems of our affluent society are quite different today. Now it is the capricious consumer who wields a weapon, optional consumption, which manifestly often leads to significant change and development.
One of the problems we discover is that many shoppers do not know how to buy. This has been spelled out most eloquently by Robert Millar in his book, "The Affluent Sheep", which discusses British buying habits. The affluent sheep, the British consumers, have money to spend but do not know how to spend it. The greatest need, apparently, is for consumer guidance. Incidentally it was the Conservative party in the United Kingdom which set up the Molony committee which studied this problem in a fresh and interesting way. The same weakness more or less is to be found in North America's affluent society, as analysed by Vance Packard in "The Hidden Persuaders". That book speaks of the new jungle called the supermarket.
It is clear that those who have given the most serious study to this field of marketing feel that there is abundant need for a department of consumer and corporate affairs. The fact is that the job of protecting the consumer has been scattered throughout many departments. A study in the United States indicates that 83 separate departments of government are concerned with this problem. Many of these departments lack adequate research facilities and cannot look into consumer problems. In this country before now there has been no single voice at a sufficiently high level in the government to speak on behalf of consumers. Now we have an able and articulate voice that will do just that.
There has been, until now, no system for bringing about a coherent consolidation of matters affecting consumer interests. The minister will serve as a high level public
4408	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs relations officer who is a go-between between the government and organizations who are trying to do something to improve our economy. All these considerations point irresistably to the wisdom of establishing a single agency of government for the protection of the consumers' interest. Actually, Canadian Labour of October, 1963, stated:
All evidence points to the fact that more money spent on consumer services by the federal government would provide a bountiful return in improved health safety, nutrition and cash savings for Canadian consumers.
In Canada on the average we spend 23 per cent of our income on food, 19.9 per cent for shelter, 10.5 per cent on transportation-that in the main means a car-and the fourth item is clothing on which we spend 8 per cent. I should like to leave those figures with the committee for its consideration.
A few weeks ago I was able to talk to an interesting personality, John Kenneth Galbraith, who was speaking at Queen's University. He has developed a new idea in economics and he talks about the concept of "countervailing power". That is what our minister had in mind in this balanced bill which has been brought to the consideration of the house. Galbraith develops the theme about the problem of prices in the modern industrial system.
Neoclassical economists like Paul Samuel-son hold that the consumer is king, that he knows what he wants and goes after it. The accepted sequence of such economists has been the unidirectional flow, on instruction from the consumer, to the market and to the producer. The provocative question is now asked, what if that flow should be reversed? Galbraith throws up this challenge in his interesting book "The New Industrial State", which deals with the new circumstances of today. What if the flow of direction and control should be reversed? What if the flow is from the producer to the market and in turn to the consumer? Can we believe in a new technological industrial system which attempts to manage the consumer, which in effect synthesizes consumption.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Actually ours has proved to be a very prosperous system. I could not deny that the United States has done more for its people than any other country in the world, and Canada comes a very close second. In these circumstances, then, part of the countervailing power which perhaps is needed to restore the balance to which I have been

DEBATES	November 17, 1967
referring is precisely the presence of specialists within government who tend to speak and act on behalf of consumers as a class.
In the last analysis, the greatest corporation must be the servant of the consumer and the consumer is the real boss; the businessman really carries out his order. This is the general view. Consumer sovereignty is sometimes spoken of as balloting in the marketplace. Yet some of the finest conceptual thinkers in the field of economic theory today-I mention by way of example Franklin Fisher and Carl Casey-detach themselves from full acceptance of the notion of consumer sovereignty. They recognize this framework described by Samuelson and others but feel there may need to be a countervailing force on the part of the state to assist the consumer to achieve a selection of purposes, to assist in obtaining clear, honest advertising, to cut waste in every possible way, and thereby to preserve and to enlarge real freedom.
This means, according to Galbraith's analysis, that we simply do not live under a pure system of competition. Joan Robinson many years ago made it clear to us that we were really living under conditions of monopolistic competition. Industry in a modern state is never entirely monopolistic; it is bound to respond to various competitive forces, notably those forces which generate from outside the country in the form of competition from multilateral trade. At the same time, however, it may synthesize consumption, control its consumers to some extent through credit agencies, through advertising and so on. Galbraith sees the sequence of planning production, distribution and sales to meet industrial rather than consumer needs.
What we are trying to do, I think, in this new department, is develop expertise to serve consumer and investment interests as they relate to corporations, to develop in Canada a sophisticated countervailing influence to benefit every single person, whether just born or about to retire or to die. Every person in Canada may be served by this consumer specialist and corporation specialist sitting in a position of influence within the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want the committee and the minister to realize that I speak as an old socialist who found himself at one time in a situation described to some extent in this bill. I have lived in complete independence and security all my life, slightly above the social welfare level, until I was elected a member of parliament, so I can well understand the situation mentioned by the minister in his recent speech to the Ot-tawa-Carleton Liberal Association.
This is a bill to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs. I think it could also be termed a bill to reconcile the contradictions of capitalism. Or it could be called a bill to handcuff free enterprise for the benefit of consumers. It might even be called a bill to experiment in participation with the consumers of Canada. It is, I think, correct to say that this is more or less experimental legislation.
In the light of all the circumstances, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs would say, and realizing the difficulties which arise with respect to the constitutional problem as between the federal government and the provinces, I am hopeful that this measure will be of some advantage to the consumers of Canada. I may say in this connection that I have received support for the bill on this basis from some of my constituents. We all realize the constitutional problems which need to be resolved and which can only be resolved with co-operation between the federal government and the provinces and the various agencies related thereto. So far as the administration is concerned, this will obviously require close co-operation among any advisory council which is to be appointed, consumers organizations across Canada and all other governmental and private agencies which are willing to take part in an effort to make this legislation a success.
I have risen to speak particularly on one aspect of this matter which concerns me. I believe that the greatest step forward with respect to the control of prices is likely to be
Corporate and Consumer Affairs through the provision of information and education in an attempt to establish better buying habits on the part of those who lack such habits at the present time. I will tell you why I say this. My wife, at the present time, bakes her own bread. She does so because she enjoys homemade bread. However, she has worked it out carefully and finds that it costs just half as much as bakers' bread. I think it would be a good thing to point out such things to members of the consuming public who require information of this type.
The other day a friend of mine was in a chain store. A lady came along, obviously of extremely modest station judging from her dress, and he noticed she had seven packets of breakfast food in the basket she was pushing around the store. She explained that she had seven children and that each of them liked a different kind of breakfast food. I think it would have been much better had she told her children: Here is a bowl of porridge, eat it, it will do you more good.
There has to be education. There has to be a measure of self-discipline if consumers hope to spend their dollars to the best advantage. The minister was kind enough to give me the notes of his speech to the Ottawa-Carleton Liberal Association entitled "The Troubled Consumer In An Affluent Society". I had an opportunity to read the speech quickly and I want to say at once that I am in accord with many of the statements made by the minister as well as with the proposals he sets out. I want to say without any question at all that I have a great deal of confidence in the minister's ability and if he gets the co-operation of the Canadian people and of all the parties in the house I am sure something can be done to improve the circumstances which we are dealing with this afternoon. On page 12, under the heading "The Troubled Consumer", I read:
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
Under the new department of corporate and consumer affairs which is presently being considered by parliament, we have an opportunity of opening a second front on the federal war on poverty.
This new department will have the power to coordinate federal consumer programs, provide effective consumer protection in matters of fraud, restrictive trade and safety, provide information and research on consumer issues, and in general develop programs to enable the consumers of this nation to gain maximum value for the full range of goods and services they purchase and use. This is an important mandate, and one that can be of special use to the many groups of low income, handicapped consumers-the troubled consumers.
November 17, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
I agree with that approach and I congratulate the minister on giving some thought to the application of this legislation to the circumstances we face at the present time. Then he goes on to say:
For those trapped in the web of poverty it is crucial that they gain maximum use of their income, but they are the ones least likely to have the capacity to do so.
That is true. I have personal experience of that sort of thing.
As study after study shows it is the poor who pay more for consumer goods of lower quality than the average Canadian housewife.
It is the low income consumer who must resort to high cost credit, with little protection or guidance.
How true that is. How often people, unfortunately because of their ignorance, enter into credit arrangements that keep them in poverty for years on end.
It is the resident of our urban or rural ghettos who doesn't have access to outlets where comparative shopping, and a wide range of goods are available.
Everyone knows that those circumstances are described correctly.
It is the uneducated and unsophisticated who are taken in by the unscrupulous seller, who fall prey to unethical advertising, and who too readily get caught in the special kinds of commercial jungles that are spawned on exploitation and fraud.
You know, Mr. Chairman, that phrase reminds me of the early days of the C.C.F. I have heard C.C.F. speakers repeatedly use that type of language, and I congratulate the minister on recognizing the fact that exploitation does exist.

speechtext: The C.C.F. doesn't.

speechtext:
The C.C.F. is alive in the N.D.P. and exploitation still exists. The minister goes on:
As a Yale Law Journal study states, "In reality the poor buy different goods and services at different stores for different prices, and this has a profound effect on their standard of living-compounding, preserving and deepening their poverty."
That is a very careful analysis of what is happening today.
That study goes on to point out that:
1.	Often it is less expensive to help a family save a given amount through proper consumer behaviour than to help them achieve an equal increase in income.
That is true, especially if the people who are trained have sound buying habits as the result of education and information.
2.	Many of the people not reached by present anti-poverty efforts could be helped by a consumer program, and

3.	The benefits of increased income may be dissipated through poor spending habits.
Therefore, anti-poverty efforts must not only aim at raising income but also at increasing the amount and quality of goods which that income provides.
I think there is tremendous scope there for co-operation with the various organizations which I have suggested and which are suggested in the minister's speech. Then he goes on to say:
In a society so oriented toward the consumption of consumer goods, where so much emphasis is placed on the possession of things-
It is not only the poor people who place emphasis on that. It is the philosophy of the society in which we live.
-and where there is such a high degree of stimulation, the consumer is faced with the bewildering, tantalizing need to grasp the nearest shiny object-a problem of special severity for the family on limited income. The Canadian living in poverty is placed at great psychological disadvantage in our modern marketplace. He has $10,000 worth of desires-
Stimulated desires, of course.
-$5,000 worth of needs, and $2,000 worth of income. This inequality leads to strange and unfortunate situations.
I am sure most members of the house have seen circumstances exactly like that. In terms of what my comrades would call my Victorian philosophy of life, I might say I am a revolutionary conservative but I have seen situations like that. I was talking to a lady not long ago, with a relatively low income, not as low as described here, who told me she never darned her children's underwear when holes appeared in it. She just threw the underwear out. You cannot endorse that sort of thing whether you are on the poverty level, above the poverty level, or well off. There has got to be knowledge, responsibility and a certain amount of self-discipline.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is quite factual and truthful to say that the other parties are tearing leaves out of all our programs. When I hear Conservatives suggest
November 17, 1967

the socialization of the C.P.R. and even of its subsidiaries, as I did last session, and hear Liberals suggest the nationalization or socialization of Dosco, I do not think there is a very great ideological gulf between many of us today. It is what we are trying to do that counts, not the sort of technical language we may use. I continue with the minister's speech in which he has outlined a consumer program.
He said:
It is for this reason that my own department sees as a first priority the need to mobilize government activity to aid the low income consumer.
1.	One obvious answer is information and education. The effects of having more accurate information about products, of knowing where to buy and how to buy and what to buy is an essential condition of making better use of income. Going beyond this, there is a striking need just to begin developing better shopping habits, of teaching consumer skills that are appropriate for the modern marketplace. This would involve counselling and neighbourhood improvement clinics-
I think that is a very good suggestion indeed.
-which would be established in conjunction with provinces, universities and private groups already working in the field.
I can imagine that the consumer organizations would be only too willing to get right in there and work in co-operation with the minister and his officials.
To begin work in this field officials in my department have begun planning a pilot project for consumer counselling. What we have in mind is to recruit the services of retired men and women who have an interest and background in economic or commercial affairs willing to donate their time to public service.
I think that is a creative suggestion and I am sure there are retired persons with knowledge and experience in life who would welcome an opportunity to undertake this type of work. I can think of some in my own district, and I will talk to the minister about that later.
