I do not like the political inference. I continue reading from the minister's speech:
Such individuals may be former businessmen, union or co-op officials, school teachers who would wish to serve in local communities as initiators of a program of consumer counselling. This person would be available to give advice on matters of credit, real estate dealing-
That is very necessary.
-legal protection-

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
A most necessary thing.
-buying skills and financial management. Most important, they would work with existing agencies in the area such as credit unions, settlement houses, fraternal organizations, church and welfare organizations with a view to establishing consumer programs of counselling, information and training particularly relevant to the needs of low income consumers. In this way they can act as a catalyst for local community action to repair consumer inequalities.
I think those are very constructive suggestions.
Our pilot project will select two or three communities initially and, if successful, can be expanded using the services of dedicated, skilled individuals who have retired from their own occupations. The provinces would naturally have to play an important part in this scheme for it to be successful.
There is no question that if this legislation is going to be successful it has to have the willing co-operation of the provinces and the participation of other organizations and individuals.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
2.	Our plans also include far more stringent and effective enforcement of the laws dealing with matters of fraud, misrepresentation and restraint of trade. There must be better protection against unethical business practices. We need the co-operation of the provinces to fashion a co-ordinated and efficient system.
I think that is very necessary and fundamental.
3.	Finally, the very presence of a consumer-oriented department in government gives us the opportunity to enact new legislation and influence the development of new policies that can improve the position of the new consumer. The proposed action on drugs is an example. There will be others in the fields of packaging, labelling, weights and measures, misleading advertising, safety, etc.
I think that before making his speech the minister perhaps listened carefully to some of the speeches made by members in this group throughout the years. If he did, I give him credit for going to the right source to gather together the best information available.
These general programs I outline are, of course, only one part of the over-all approach required by the existence of millions of "troubled", low-income consumers, both those caught in poverty, and those who because of age, or youthful inexperience, or lack of consumer skills, find the market place restrictive to their ambitions, rather than the asset it should be. No one level of government can provide all the answers and there must be the concerted and co-ordinated involvement of the provinces, municipalities, schools, churches and private groups which have a stake in the consumer's battle.
November 17, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
That is definitely so.
Poverty like war is a complex of problems that will not surrender to scattered action. There must be a dedicated, unified response utilizing the best resources and best minds in the country.
So when we talk about the challenges open to us in this new century, when we think of the greatness that can be ours, we must think in terms of how we build a society open to all citizens, spreading its advantages throughout the population.
That is the philosophy of this group.
The troubled consumer is, of course, only one dimension of the total program of problem solving required in the next generation. There is a large inventory of other issues-the state of our cities-
I quite agree with this.
-the rational development of our resources, the proper use of new communication and new technology, the direction of our foreign policy.
We in this group consider this to be most important.
Each of these require the full mobilization of power and effort in the Canadian community.
I have quoted at length from the minister's speech because I was very pleased to see that he had given some thought to these things which are of advantage to the country as a whole and the people whom we seek to serve. In conclusion I should like to wish the minister every success in the administration of this legislation. I realize it is somewhat experimental in nature, but we trust that as the years go by it will be to the great advantage of the Canadian consumer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, permit me to contribute in passing Bill No. C-161, which will be significant in the future, even though it is claimed that such a department should have been set up during previous parliaments.
I was somewhat surprised to hear the encomiums of the house philosopher, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), in contrast to the criticism of certain members of the opposition. Since the minister has the blessings of our great philosopher, I am sure this new legislation will succeed. I agree unreservedly with certain qualities that some hon. members have bestowed upon the incumbent of the new department, but I nevertheless wish him courage, boldness and determination to carry out the program he has laid down. Before taking my seat, I propose to remind him of certain objectives which he has set for himself and of the methods he has outlined during his speech on second reading.

If I am particularly concerned with the bill now before us, Mr. Chairman, it is because I represent a constituency largely made up of workers whose family budget is somewhat limited. I could state that approximately 30 per cent of the people in my constituency live in a state of hardship, want or poverty. I am convinced that the new department of corporate and consumer affairs will do much to enable the housewife to make the best possible use of the available budget.
In the last few years particularly, there has been talk of waging war on poverty. This war on poverty should not be waged only with money and all kinds of subsidies. Social assistance measures, social security measures, assistance to housing must be provided of course, but care must also be taken that subsidies will be used in the best possible way by those who receive them and in this, the new department can do a great deal.
I consider most important the role the new department will play in the field of merchandising. A great quantity of products are offered to the public and the various advertising techniques often risk misleading the consumers. As a matter of fact, when shopping, a housewife must often give much thought and make many calculations to be sure of the quality and quantity of the items she buys. The various representations made by housewives in the last few years prove that a problem exists, and I am glad to note that the new department of corporate and consumer affairs intends to control very closely manufacturers' advertising, and see to it that goods are honestly and completely described.
The department will have to keep a sharp eye on radio and television advertising. Some ads are in bad taste and, above all, create new needs for families. I know quite well that the ultimate purpose of advertising is to promote products to attract consumers. But should we not consider imposing limitations on advertising? Is it desirable, for instance, to advertise a cigarette brand by implying that fashionable people, the boy who is with it, must smoke such a brand? Can we accept that a certain beer should be advertised by suggesting that, when things go wrong, the best way to get out of trouble is to drink that beer?
In that field of advertising, I wish to protest particularly against advertising intended for children. For instance, now the holiday season is coming on. Every year, parents with limited means complain about the fact that some televised programs for children
November 17, 1967

involve a form of advertising which leads the child to ask for the most expensive toys. The little girl does not merely want any doll for Christmas; she demands a doll which does all kinds of special tricks and which, of course, is very expensive. If the parents cannot afford to buy the doll which was advertised, Christmas day will be disappointing, even if the parents have made great sacrifice to offer their children the toys they could afford. To me, that publicity is but odious blackmail. I would suggest that the new department consider forbidding publicity aimed directly at children, by virtue of the principle that they are not responsible, are easily influenced and unable to understand the need to limit their demands to the possibilities of the family budget.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The department to be created by Bill No. C-161 can contribute a lot to educating the consumer. There again, the experience of the people in my riding enables me to see the numerous possibilities in that field. Where a couple barely has enough for the basic needs, the ability of the mother to manage the family budget can mean the difference between a happy family and a poverty-stricken family. The women consumers must be taught to plan their budget; they must be taught to save, to choose their products and to set up the priorities in the needs of the family.
How should we educate housewives? By means of various publications, radio and television spot announcements, even contacts between housewives and management experts. Some thought could be given, perhaps, to setting up, in less fortunate areas, information centres where housewives could be instructed in budget planning and the best possible use of the limited funds available. Furthermore, such centres could be a clearing house for housewives' complaints against fraudulent advertising or excessive price ranges; housewives could even voice their suggestions to these centres, which would pass them on to the department of corporate and consumer affairs, as suggested by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Gray).
Such a campaign for consumer education should not be limited to adults. The department should also educate teen-agers who spend lavishly the first dollars they earn. I come back to the idea I expressed a moment ago: some persons may receive many pensions, several welfare cheques, but if they do not know how to manage their budget, they will always remain as poor and their family will always be indigent.
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
To conclude, I want to emphasize the task which the department of consumer and corporate affairs will have to perform in the field of credit. I could give a list of many families in my riding which have been defrauded, not to say robbed, by finance companies or door to door salesmen who bring to bear too much sales pressure often on credit, for goods of very dubious quality.
The future head of that department mentioned the reports of the Economic Council which point out that, as a whole, the general provisions of the Criminal Code against fraudulent sales practices constitute, on the part of the federal government, a key legislation to protect the consumer. I am happy to note that the future department will co-ordinate the application of the various measures to protect the consumer against lenders whose honesty is often questionable. There again the department of corporate and consumer affairs will be able to educate the consumers. It is necessary to let the people know, especially those with a low income, about the danger of borrowing too often and too much.
In my remarks, I stressed mainly the role of educator that the future department will play. I am convinced that many people are living in misery because they lack information on all kinds of things and cannot get the most out of the money at their disposal.
The new department, Mr. Chairman, also includes the corporations but, as I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, I intend to speak of consumer affairs only.
Before concluding, I should like to remind the head of this new department of the goals he had established and the course he intended to follow in his new department. This is excellent, in my opinion, at least at the beginning, and it will help to control and perhaps stop, for some time at least, this price increase about which all the housewives are complaining.
Here is what the minister said, as shown on pages 3232 and 3233 of the official report of last October 18:
Our goals are simple, and I wish to summarize them.
I am greatly encouraged to see that the minister is taking things so well and that he seems certain of the future of his department, because his list of goals is quite long. In fact, he has a great many. As he seems to be so very hopeful, I wish him all the success in the world and, as I said at the beginning, his courage and determination will help him
November 17, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs to reach his goals. I continue to quote from his speech:
We wish to ensure, first, that the Canadian as a consumer is afforded full protection against fraud, deception and unfair trade practices; second, that he is offered the maximum standards of quality, safety and protection in the services and goods he buys; third, that he is provided with full and accurate information on which to base his purchases; fourth, that he is given strong and active representation in the councils of government; fifth, that he becomes involved in debates and discussions on those decisions affecting his vital consumer interests; sixth, that he is able to make maximum use of the amazing storehouse of riches in the Canadian market. To do this, we are trying to build a department that will, first, make use of the best of modern organizational and program methods to get the best value for the dollar spent in government services.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I hope the department will be set up as soon as possible, in order to help those who, according to certain figures, make up between 30 and 40 per cent of our population. As I said at the beginning, in my own riding, whose population is mostly made up of the working class, at least 30 per cent of the people are deprived of the necessities of life. I venture to hope that, thanks to the measures to be taken, these people will now be protected against a certain exaggerated publicity and that it will be possible to teach them to draw up their budget in the best possible way, so as to regenerate family life.

This is one of the factors which will have to change very soon if those hon. members wish to achieve greater success.

speechtext: That is good advice coming from one from your part of the country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
The amendment before us at the present time strikes me as being a mistake. I opposed the resolution introducing this bill to set up a department of consumer affairs on the grounds that it was not really

necessary. I now find that the amendment is compounding that error.
Let me enlarge on the reasons for my feeling that it is an error and a compounding of an error. One of the things the Registrar General will have to learn during his rapidly advancing political career is how to recognize an attack. Certain qualities he brings with him to his political career, which were outlined to the house the other evening by the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas and I shall not repeat them at this time caused people such as the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway to rush to his assistance. That hon. lady rushed to his assistance the other day when we were debating the resolution. She had some suggestions for him which she felt were important. In any event he should recognize an attack, no matter how attractively packaged, advertised or presented. I know of no one who can do these things better than the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. As a result, I am afraid he accepted one suggestion she presented the other afternoon and it appears now in the amendment.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I think the emphasis here is most dangerous. The hon. member for Yukon has pointed out correctly that the amendment is phony. He did a very good job of pointing out in the debate on the resolution that the legislation is phony. I have to agree with the hon. member when he says this. I suppose what the amendment will do is fool some of the public a little more into assuming that the government, by laying its massive hand on various aspects of industry, will actually protect the public. This is something I very much doubt.
I was impressed by an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of last Wednesday. It was written by Mr. Bruce Hutchison who at the present time works out of my province. The article is entitled "World Corporations Seen As Way To Revolutionizing Life." Mr. Hutchison bases his article on conversations he had with Anthony Wedgwood Benn and George W. Ball during a recent trip to Britain. I should like to quote at some length from the article because I believe it contains some things which are very pertinent to the amendment and the bill before us this afternoon. Mr. Hutchison says that Mr. Wedgwood Benn:
-begins with the remarkable pledge that the Labour government is totally committed to "the success and profitability" of private enterprise in Britain. He adds that "no previous British government, of any party, has hitherto entered into such a commitment."
November 17, 1967

Of course, he has correctly defined the political situation in Britain at the present time, where the government that calls itself Labour is nothing of the kind but is working in any way it can to stave off a disaster that has been at least partially produced by the excesses of the policies for which Labour has usually stood. The article goes on to say:
While the British economy must always be "mixed," with deep intervention by the state, "the profitability of a mixed economy is an essential prerequisite of economic growth and commercial success." So much for the myth of pure "socialism" and the evils of profit still nourished by a dwindling group of nostalgic socialists of Canada.
I feel that this bill and the amendment are part of the last gasp in Canada of that approach to profit. Mr. Wedgwood Benn did not stop there, because the article continues:
But Mr. Wedgwood Benn lifts it to a new and unfamiliar level where the thinking of the Canadian government, the Opposition and the New Democratic party has not yet arrived.
You notice, Mr. Chairman, that the Social Credit party was omitted there, because we arrived at approximately this level back in 1935 and have stayed there ever since. The article goes on to say:
In a word, he has grasped the fact that modem technology is basically revolutionizing the world economy, and man's entire way of life, in a totally unexpected fashion and making most of his economic and political notions quite obsolete.
This is the appeal I make to the minister this afternoon, namely, that he recognize an obsolete suggestion when it is handed to him. I refer to the suggestion that we set up a department purporting to protect the consumer and then this afternoon go through the legerdemain of shifting the title around. We must recognize that this will not protect the consumer. We must also recognize the obsolescence of the approach in which the minister and the government are involved at the present time. This article goes on to say:
The first phase of this revolution proclaims itself in vast, privately owned international corporations, most of them based in the United States. Already "they have established such superiority over their international competitors that no single European country, even if it merged every company in a single field into one monolithic industrial group, could alone stand against them. I am certain that corporations like those hold the future of the world's high-technology industries in their hands."
Finally, we have a quotation from Mr. Ball, the other source from which the writer drew the information for his article:
With a daring but typical lunge into the unknown, Mr. Ball proposes some international authority, established by treaty, to license and control the
Corporate and Consumer Affairs new corporate colossi so that they may nourish man's wealth without abusing his natural rights and his differing national aspirations.
It is in this field that the problem lies. For this reason, if we must have this bill at all, and if the official opposition lies down before the challenge of the presentation of the bill, for goodness sake let us at least defeat this amendment and leave the word "corporate" as one of the first words in the title. If we are to protect the consumer now and in the future, attention must be given to the overwhelmingly important problems on the world economic scene and not to the size of the package and whether or not it has a dish towel in it.
This is why I regret that the tremendous variety of women's organizations which sprang up about a year ago to bring to governmental and public attention the abuses that were going on in this area have felt that their only objective should be to turn the whole matter over to the government. Surely any member who has sat in this House of Commons for any length of time and has had to work through the levels of governmental bureaucracy in order to solve the simplest problem knows that this is not the only way to keep track of the number of ounces in a box of soap, that an aroused public, an educated public concerned about the abuses that they wish prevented will always be needed. If we think the enormous effort of government can be focused on some of these small packages, we are looking at the wrong end of the problem altogether.
I listened this afternoon with interest as usual, to the hon. member for Kootenay West who gave us a variety of examples where the public has not been sufficiently educated or sufficiently careful in its shopping or purchasing habits. The hon. member referred to a lady from this area who confessed to being negligent in repairing her children's underwear. I was rather surprised that he should have raised this sensitive topic in the house at this time, but he did. One really cannot mind that because the hon. member for Kootenay West always looks after his constituents in a way that any member could well copy.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The only thing I criticize is his conclusion. He seemed to feel that the good lady should get busy with needle and thread and that he should in some way reprimand her for a statement that he found surprising. I would say to him and to all the members of the
November 17, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs party he represents that they should "get with it" just a bit. He should have recommended the lady as a recipient of the centennial medal for her contribution to the Canadian economy because she is on the right track. We know that manufacturers have given us great variety, usefulness, beauty and ease in our present society, articles such as instant coffee, paper tissues, automobiles, and other products which move us and assist us. Within two years they will be providing us with disposable underwear which the good lady will not need to darn nor wash because it will be made of paper.
The hon. member for Kootenay West should recognize the great economic advantage to his own constituency of such a move. This is part of the technological revolution described in this article. Especially in view of the construction of the vast hydroelectric projects and in view of the vast forest resources of his constituency, the hon. member should write a letter of commendation to the lady for being ahead of her time. Perhaps she is approaching the immediate situation in a rather uneconomical way but she is looking to the future which is coming sooner than we think.

Yes, of course, but the farsighted policies of the Social Credit government of British Columbia have placed forest reserves on most of the lands in the province which are unfit for agriculture and in fact have moved some of the marginal land which was unfit for agriculture back into forest reserves. Therefore in really vast areas of the province we must be concerned not about the agricultural industry, which is important to some parts of his constituency and very important to mine, but with the forest industry.
Last of all, Mr. Chairman, I suggest there is a strange anomaly in this government moving in a variety of pseudo fashions to present itself as the great protector of the consumer and at the same time enabling the introduction of lotteries on the Canadian scene, because if anything removes purchasing power from the hands of the consumers who need it most lotteries will do it. If we pass this bill this afternoon and it becomes the law of the land, we shall have to take a very good look at the other bill when it comes before us.

Mr. Chairman, as usual the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke applied a new version of the twist to the words I used when I rose last to speak very briefly and appealed to hon. members to pass this legislation as well as the other two pieces of legislation listed for discussion today. His speeches are usually pompous and most of them are empty of content, empty of any constructive contribution and completely devoid of any thinking. Perhaps if he could stop the practice of mumbling in his beard we might understand him. I will simply say that his speeches can be compared to a steer. They have a point on each side with a lot of bull in between.
I say once again that we on this side are prepared to deal conclusively with this legislation this afternoon. It was first debated on June 16 when the minister's estimates were being considered and later on October 7, October 18 and October 19. The hon. member who has just interjected, and who usually interjects at what he considers to be appropriate times when it would be much better for him to keep quiet, should not speak about my attendance here which I would compare at any time with the attendance of 99 per cent of the members of his party who today are conspicuous by their absence.
The bill now before us is an important one. I join with some of my colleagues who have expressed their concern and disapproval of the idea of placing under one department and one minister the responsibility of protecting the interests of the consumers and the responsibility of regulating corporations. It seems to me it is like putting a lamb and a lion in one pit. We know who survives in that kind of situation.
It seems to me also that the corporations have enough representation in the house. They have good representation in the Department of Trade and Commerce and they have good friends in the Department of Industry, as they should. I think that the consumers of this country could well have a department in which the minister and his staff would have one job, to protect the interests of the consumers.
Our society works through various groups which organize and band together to make their views and desires known to governments and to the community as a whole. This is as it should be. The working people of this country are represented by their trade unions and by two trade union federations. The manufacturers are represented by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. The farmers are represented by the National
Corporate and Consumer Affairs Farmers' Union and by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I could go on naming the interest groups which have representation and organizations. When something happens that affects them they are very quick to come here to tell the government and the various political parties what they think should be done. And so they should, Mr. Chairman. Unfortunately, the consumers have not been able to organize and to make their desires felt.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The proposal to set up this department is one with which the members of this party agree. We have a very young, presentable, and if one reads the press reports, a very able minister. He has been travelling across the country making speeches about what he thinks he needs to do in his job and about some of the problems faced by consumers. This is all to the good. Some of his ideas are excellent; they ought to be, because they have been put forward for a number of years.
I want to refer to some of the things that the minister indicated his department will be undertaking. Unlike my colleague from Kootenay West, I am not going to quote the minister verbatim in one of his speeches, copies of which seem to arrive on our desks three or four times a week.

speechtext: He did not make a speech at Edmonton though. We missed that.

speechtext:
That may be. I cannot keep track of them. However, I do want to quote from two articles which appeared in the Financial Post for April 15, 1967. They concern some of the things that the minister sees his department undertaking. For example, he is going to increase his investigation and research staff. The combines investigation department has been told to recruit more economists and lawyers; the actual investigation staff will probably be doubled. That is an excellent idea. I wonder what will happen to this proposal, Mr. Chairman, in light of the austerity program of the Minister of Finance.
The minister is also planning to put more teeth into our existing law. For example, if the minister has his way directors of companies who are guilty of flagrant price fixing may face criminal charges. As the minister says: "Why should only trade unionists go to jail?" That is a question I have been asking for two or three years now.
November 17. 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
1 want to know what the minister has been doing since April. Where is the legislation that will spell out the authority he is to be given to do this sort of thing? It is not on the order paper.

speechtext: He is waiting for us to pass the bill.

speechtext:
Nonsense, we do not have to pass the bill. The minister is in office and has staff, and he could have got on with it a long time ago.
There is also going to be an extension of the combines legislation to cover service industries. According to the Financial Post it is no secret that the minister would like to launch an investigation into professional sport, the activities of the National Hockey League and the Canadian Football League.
It should not be very difficult for the minister to do this, Mr. Chairman. All he has to do is to talk to the former member for York West, Mr. "Red" Kelly who, when he decided it was time to stop playing hockey and to become a coach, was told in no uncertain terms by the Toronto Maple Leafs that they owned his contract for life and that he could not do anything until they gave permission.
So I ask, where is the legislation? I remember the former member for Port Arthur, before I came to the house asked a former minister of justice when the government would amend the legislation so that it would be impossible for the National Hockey League to sign to contracts youngsters of 12 and 13 years of age, contracts which tied them to particular hockey teams for the rest of their lives, if they wanted to play hockey for gain. Talk about slavery in the United States before the civil war. We have slavery here in Canada, Mr. Chairman. Why is the minister waiting all these months before taking some action in this regard?
The article goes on to say that the legislation will open the way for injured parties in price fixing cases to sue in civil courts for damages. I remember, Mr. Chairman, when certain electric companies in the United States-Westinghouse, General Electric and several others-were prosecuted in that famous case, and some of their officers were treated like ordinary people who broke the law and sent to jail for a month, something which we have never done. I suggest the minister should look at this possibility. I cannot think of anything which would make directors and officers of Canadian corporations think more seriously about obeying our laws than this kind of action, instead of
['Mr. Orlikow.]
patting them over the wrist with a $25,000 fine.
When this action was taken in the United States, Mr. Chairman, it was followed up with something even more salutary. It was followed by the electric utility companies, both co-operative and private, going to the courts of the United States and suing these large companies which had mulcted them and the public, by fixing rates far higher than they ought to for generators and other equipment which the electric utilities had to buy. The companies were sued in the courts for the amounts which these utility companies felt they had overpaid. Speaking from memory-and I think I am correct-under United States law I think you are permitted to sue not only for damages but for triple damages. The minister is kind enough to help me by confirming what I say. I ask once again, where is the draft of this legislation? Why is it not on the order paper?
I could continue to quote from the article, but I think I have made my point, Mr. Chairman. The minister has said all the right things, and they are very nice to hear. Perhaps they help him a great deal in his quest for the leadership of the Liberal party. I do not mind if he is successful in that quest; I am not too worried about that; but I do wish he would spend some time in Ottawa running his department. I wish the minister would get on with his job.

order paper and debated in the house over a period of many years dealing with this subject, the government finally got busy and established the joint committee on consumer credit. This report was tabled in February of this year. I am not going to read the whole report because it runs to well over 100 pages, but there are some very specific recommendations made in the report in respect to changes in the legislation which, if adopted, would protect to a large extent the ordinary people in this country. I just want to give one illustration of the kind of robbery-I realize, of course, it is not legal robbery- that affects people who can ill afford it.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The Financial Post of three or four years ago carried the story of a recently landed immigrant who became the victim of a mortgage broker. He borrowed and received $1,500 from the broker, but to get that amount he had to sign a note and promise to repay $2,350. The extra $850 represented the arranging fee. After paying the prescribed $35 a month for three years the immigrant found that he still owed $1,580, which was more than the amount he had originally borrowed. He thought he was paying an interest rate of 7 per cent, but the actual interest rate turned out to be 30 per cent.
This instance is not new, nor is it isolated. There are thousands like it every year. That is the sort of thing which the joint committee on consumer credit looked at and made recommendations about. I shall read into the record a few of those recommendations. The first one, to be found on page 3 of the report on consumer credit, reads as follows:
We endorse the principle of what is popularly known as "truth in lending": that is, the principle embodied in the disclosure bills that have been repeatedly introduced in the Senate and in the House of Commons. Specifically, we recommend that every person, firm or corporation, including every chartered bank, carrying on the business of extending consumer credit, shall be required by law to disclose to the consumer the total cost of that credit, expressed both as a lump sum and in terms of simple annual interest.
The second recommendation reads:
The principle of "truth in lending" should be extended to provide protection for all potential 27053-279
Corporate and Consumer Affairs borrowers, whether or not they are at the point of committing themselves to a purchase or a loan. For this reason it is essential that all advertising of credit should truthfully and accurately state the total cost of the credit to the consumer.
Stopping there for a moment, Mr. Chairman, I wish to tell the minister that in discussing these matters previously I have illustrated my remarks by referring to advertisements which appeared in Winnipeg newspapers. I am sure that similar advertisements appear in newspapers of other cities. I am speaking of advertisements which urge people to borrow up to $5,000 and which say that repayments are to be as little as $50 a month. One is not told for how many months he must pay. I suggest to the minister, and I agree with the committee, that this kind of advertising is immoral, unjust and ought to be stopped.
The fourth recommendation of the committee was the following:
We recommend that the Parliament of Canada extend the protection accorded to borrowers under the Small Loans Act so as to include loans up to $5,000 rather than loans up to $1,500, with appropriate interest ceilings.
The sixth recommendation is:
Consumers are sometimes compelled to pay for faulty or defective goods, or even for goods they never receive. This is particularly hard on the consumer when, as occasionally happens, the purchaser of his obligation to pay has no knowledge of the original transaction. To prevent situations of that kind, we recommend that every bill or note given in connection with a retail credit transaction be required to be so marked on its face.
I could go on and on because the committee brought in many excellent and essential recommendations. But where are they reflected in the legislation? I know that in the area of consumer credit the jurisdiction is divided between the federal government and the provinces. I also know that a number of provinces already have acted on the basis of this study and on the basis of their own studies. Speaking from memory, I think I am right in saying that in this area of consumer matters the province of Nova Scotia has passed legislation, as have the provinces of Manitoba and Ontario. But where is the federal legislation?
Apart from the time the minister spends campaigning for the Liberal leadership he ought to devote his full time to working out the details of this legislation.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill has been a perennial with me. I first introduced a similar bill in 1963, followed by one in all subsequent sessions since. I notice the bill is numbered C-13 this time. I do not know whether that is significant one way or the other.

The explanatory notes in the bill are quite clear. At the present time the Criminal Code of Canada makes it illegal to disseminate any information designed to prevent conception, and this has been on the statutes in the Criminal Code since 1892. I should like to say at the outset that this bill does not deal with abortion in any way at all. This is a distinctly separate subject which is being studied at the present time by the health and welfare committee. The bill simply deals with birth control or family planning, whichever term is preferable. The meaning of the present law is quite clear. It is against the law to give such information, and in recent years the law has fallen into disuse. Prosecutions have been infrequent. I believe the last one was in 1961.
As we all know, physicians regularly give advice on this subject, as well as prescriptions. Druggists sell materials, public health nurses give information, and hospitals, both public and private, supply birth control information to various people. Many cities and counties in Canada are now openly engaged in this practice. Indeed, last year, with the authorization of the minister of health in the province of Ontario, family planning services were made available in the public health clinics of that province. The city of Montreal is now providing this type of service to the citizens of that city. However, as the law reads at the present time, all these people are breaking the law, and that would include also the government of Canada which has purchased contraceptive materials.
My colleague, the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schreyer) asked a question which was answered on June 21, 1967. His question, No. 187, reads as follows:
1.	What were the government of Canada expenditures in each of the last two fiscal years for purposes of purchasing supplies of drugs and devices of a contraceptive nature?
2.	By what departments were these expenditures made and what was the amount in each case?
3.	From what drug manufacturing or distribution firms were these purchases made?
In the reply which the hon. member received from the Department of National Defence the amounts were stated. The only point I wish to stress is that the government of Canada is breaking section 150(2) of the Criminal Code.

As I said, Mr. Speaker, the law has fallen into disuse. There have been very few prosecutions-none that I know of since 1961. In these matters that affect the private lives of individuals we in Canada always seem to lag behind other countries. The social mores change but we do not seem to change very quickly. For example, on the subject of divorce, we have studied the subject and made recommendations, but as yet we have no legislation to implement those recommendations. We are at least 30 to 35 years behind everyone else.
Almost every other country in the western world has changed its law on this particular subject of the dissemination of information on birth control. I want to give an illustration of one country that has moved rather fast on the subject, and I am referring to France. France had on the statute books a law almost identical to the one in Canada. In the French presidential campaign of November, 1965 M. Mitterand, one of the candidates, raised this question. There was quite a popular response to it on the part of the French electorate, and early in 1966, shortly after the election, the French national assembly appointed a commission to study the subject. This commission, headed by a French deputy, M. Lucien Nieuwirth, reported early in 1967, and in June 1967 the French assembly actually changed the law of France. All of this happened, Mr. Speaker, within the space of a little more than a year and a half.
I want to give a little background to what has happened in Canada. The first bill that I introduced on this subject and the first bill on the subject to be introduced in the house was in 1963. Following its introduction there was quite a campaign for public support by various groups within the country. But as often happens with private bills, it did not come up for second reading in the session of 1963.
I reintroduced the bill in 1964 and it was actually debated on September 11,	1964.
There is an interesting little story in connection with this. It is very seldom that a private member's bill ever passes in the House of Commons. One had passed earlier that year, a bill introduced by the present Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Saint Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), to change the name of Trans-Canada Air Lines to Air Canada. By some agreement that got through.

I found out later they had misunderstood the bill; they thought it dealt with the subject of abortion, which it did not. However, the bill failed passage in 1964 and it has not been debated in the house since.
Following the new parliament which came after the election of November 1965 four bills were introduced in the house on the subject, one by myself, one by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford), one by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) and one by the hon. member for York-Scarbor-ough (Mr. Stanbury). All four bills were subsequently referred to the committee on health and welfare.
That committee held a series of hearings and heard from all interested parties who wanted to appear. I should like to read the list of the national and local organizations which appeared before that committee. The Anglican Church of Canada, the Association des Medecins de Langue Francais du Canada, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Catholic Conference, the Canadian Unitarian Council, the Canadian Welfare Council, the Community Welfare Planning Council of Manitoba, the Consumers Association of Canada, the Family Planning Federation of Canada, the National Council of Women, the Pentecostal Assemblies of Canada, an organization known as SERENA of Ottawa, the United Church of Canada, the Voice of Women of Canada and the Y.W.C.A. of Canada. All of these groups except the Pentecostal Assemblies of Canada gave support to the idea, though some of them with qualifications. The committee on health and welfare reported to the house, and I want to refer briefly to their report which is dated Friday, November 18,	1966, a year ago
tomorrow. Part of the report is as follows:
Your committee feels that the dissemination of family planning knowledge should he completely available and free from any fear of illegality, as a matter of personal choice.


Then on the following page, page 591, the report continues:
Medical knowledge and technique are at a level today where intelligent family planning can be carried out relatively easily. The present laws of Canada have made this impossible in its fullest sense. It is the feeling of your committee that family planning is a personal decision of a married couple and the state should not interfere with action or laws in any way to influence such a personal decision.
The committee made some recommendations and I will refer to them a little later on. I want to refer briefly to the submission made to the committee by the Canadian Catholic Conference, which is a conference of the bishops of the Catholic church in Canada. In part, Mr. Speaker, they had this to say:
In the light of these conditions we consider Article 150, which forbids giving information about contraception as well as the sale or distribution of contraceptives, an inadequate law today. We consider it so quite independently of the morality or immorality of various methods of birth prevention. We believe it a deficient law because it does not meet all the conditions outlined above.
The law is not in fact enforced, and the good of public peace might well be lost by attempts to enforce it. A large number of our fellow citizens believe that this law violates their rights to be informed and helped toward responsible parenthood in accordance with their personal beliefs.
It is our clear understanding, of course, that the modification of the law in question is not to extend to that part of it which has to do with abortion. For our conclusions would be quite different were there question of such direct destruction of human life.
The church is making its view known on abortion to the health and welfare committee, but on this occasion it did agree that section 150 of the Criminal Code should be changed.
It seems to me simply incredible that here in Canada we take so long to do anything. I gave you the example of France, where within a little more than a year and a half the subject was brought out into the open, debated, studied by a French parliamentary committee and the law changed. Many people advocated this change before I came on the scene, but the first bill introduced in this house was by myself in 1963. And here we are, Mr. Speaker, in 1967, four and a half years later, and no change has been made.
To be fair, Mr. Speaker, I will say that some action has been taken on the report of the committee on health and welfare. There was introduced in the Senate on November 1 Bill No. S-22, which deals with this and a number of other subjects. In essence, Bill S-22 recommends that the section on contraception, as it now appears in the Criminal Code, be taken out. This bill also suggests

Mr. Speaker, it is said in the explanatory notes that the purpose of this bill is to exempt from the sections of the Criminal Code referring to family planning, authorized personnel of duly incorporated family planning associations, physicians, pharmacists, or registered nurses and public organizations. Authority is given to these people or organizations to legally sell or distribute means, instructions, medicine, drugs or articles intended as a method of family planning. That is the bill this house is asked to vote on.
Section 150(2)(c) of the Criminal Code is open to all sorts of omissions or transgressions and, in fact, Mr. Speaker, what is happening now is a joke. This is the section that the Canadian government itself has violated through some of its actions toward overpopulated countries. Bad legislation breeds contempt of the law itself. According to Father James R. Robarts, member of the Catholic family court of the Vancouver archdiocese, any legislation, in order to be effective and benefit the community, must be accepted by the majority of the population; otherwise, its violation by a great number of people, even in good faith, breeds contempt of the law.
In September 1964, a bill similar to the one now being considered was introduced in this house, but it failed to meet the unanimous approval of the members. I sincerely believe it is high time we looked into that problem seriously and objectively, if we are not to be accused of denying the individual of one of his most sacred rights, that of having children when he wants and in any number he wants.
According to Teilhard de Chardin, no human being worthy of the name can accept that an outside force or coercion should prevent him from fulfilling himself naturally and normally. To be a father, to be a mother is a wonderful experience, especially when parents know they can give their children all they need.
Still, births that come too close to one another can become dangerous for the mother's health. Too many children can become a heavy burden instead of a great joy. All parents want the best for their children: a good home, good food, a good education, in short, happiness. When parents plan their family, have children when they want them, the family has a better chance of being
4432	COMMONS
Amendment Respecting Birth Control happy and healthy. That is why that question must be looked into by society and especially by the family.
The essential thing is to provide for the birth of children under proper conditions and to restore to the couple the joys of freely accepted parenthood. Accordingly, there is no question of exercising mandatory control over the number of children, but to space births so that each child is born into a family that welcomes him and is able to provide for all his needs, including a proper education.
If, on the one hand, we agree that husbands and wives have an inalienable right to attain a spiritualization of love through a dialogue where they can together evolve toward a flowering of their mutual love and, on the other hand, that the child, the fruit of this love, has also the right to be born in an atmosphere and environment conducive to his education and upbringing, we must logically and inevitably infer that both parents are entitled to enlightened information on various contraceptive methods, their use and disadvantages. Furthermore, the doctor must not substitute his conscience to that of his patients by imposing his own moral standards on them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, who can get this instruction, this knowledge? Everyone who so wishes, I would say without hesitating. I would even say that sexual education should be given to children, adapting it to their capacity and development.
Later, when they have grown up, when they are adults, they will be in a better position to understand the great problems relating to the noble role of transmitting life through love freely accepted and given.
All Canadian citizens, rich as well as poor, must have free access to this knowledge which will enable them to perform in peace, love and order, their noble role of procreator intended by God.
Among the long-term measures which might help to improve the lot of needy families, Dr. Mongeau puts the amendment of the law on contraception, the opening of free family planning clinics, the extension of marriage preparation courses to more people, better training for doctors and social workers, so that they can give judicious advice on family planning, as well as a better sex education at home and in primary and secondary schools.
Who should dispense such information? Precisely those who have the competence and training required to inform the people about

such matters and who were forbidden by law to do so until now.
Only the representatives of family planning associations regularly incorporated, doctors, pharmacists or registered nurses and the public organizations would be authorized to sell or distribute legally any information, drug or article needed for family planning.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The centres authorized to distribute information on family planning should be oriented towards the essential family values and its preservation; above all, they must endeavour to consider the problems of fertility not only from its technical viewpoint, but within the context of the many conjugal problems to which birth control too often serves as a smoke screen.
At this time, one problem seems to worry many people. How will the young people react to this information on contraceptive? Will it constitute an open door to dissolute ways and the debauchery of minors? To that question, I shall reply with another. Was alcoholism ever checked by prohition laws?
Again, would we revolutionize the problem of premarital sexual relations by hiding the truth from those who thirst for it? As it stands now, the legislation barely covers up the advertising and sale of contraceptive products to which young people already have easy access whenever they wish.
Can it be properly inferred that the establishment of conjugal clinics would greatly increase the incidence of premarital sex among youths? In my estimation, only a sound sexual education can help youth to discover the true meaning of sexuality in marriage. Prohibitions and smoke-screens of all kinds can but further enhance for them the eternal attraction of the forbidden fruit.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, as the civil legislators, we must be guided by two major criteria: the natural law and the common good of the country.
Indeed, the determination and justification of any legislation must be based mainly on the natural law. In a certain sense, I think we must put aside our religious persuasion, precisely because there are so many in the country.
A civil law which is to be respected by all the citizens of a country, irrespective of their religion, cannot be based on religious prejudice, but on a principle accepted by the majority of citizens, in this case natural law. But does this mean that the legislator cannot
November 17, 1967

indirectly make use of the certain knowledge which he derives from his religion? Certainly not, but this knowledge must serve as a confirmation and not as a justification. I shall come back to this later, Mr. Speaker.
The second criterion of a civil law is the common good. Indeed, a law which would only apply to part of the population for example only to Catholics, could be called unfair towards the rest of the people, and therefore would be in no way compulsory.
These very personal remarks have been formulated in the spirit of freedom of conscience advocated by Vatican II. Freedom of conscience does not mean syncretism or eclectism, but being true to oneself, to that verdict which comes from one's very soul and which dictates how one should behave.
There is nothing like examples to explain our news, Mr. Speaker. Now, I am referring to divorce and family planning. The church is more reserved than broad-minded on those two points, and it is right, because its legislation only concerns one group of persons, to wit the Catholics. But civil society, which includes various religious faiths, must draw up legislation taking that multiplicity into account. Consequently, it seems to me that its legislation on divorce or family planning must be more broad-minded, while taking the appropriate measures to control any abuses which are always possible. And let us note that, whatever may be the broadening of such legislation, it can very well not give more freedom to such group of persons.
For instance, the broadening of the divorce law in civil court will be useless to Catholics if they are faithful to their religious convictions, essentially because divorce is not allowed by the religious court.
And, if it is not allowed by the religious court, then conscience does not allow it either in the civil court.
Here is another example, Mr. Speaker. If, for a Protestant, divorce may be granted only on grounds of adultery and if, on the other hand, his religion allows only his motive, he will not be able to petition for divorce on any other grounds, if he is faithful to his religious convictions, even if civil law allows divorce on three or four grounds other than that one.
This leads me to speak of everyone's own conscience. There is a Catholic conscience as there is a Protestant, Lutheran or Orthodox conscience. It seems to me that civil legislators should not be afraid to appeal to that

Amendment Respecting Birth Control conscience and keep returning to it often. Even if civil divorce is legal for four reasons, for instance, the fact remains that for a person in particular, divorce can be legal for only one of these reasons, his conscience formally prohibiting him to use the other three. We must keep in mind that everyone's conscience is the ultimate standard of any human action. This conscience factor is of prime importance in the face of any legislation and we, as legislators, should not be afraid to appeal to it. We may thus contribute in rousing some consciences, asleep or wavering, which are only waiting for an appeal from outside to come out of its torpor.
I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that a legislator can use indirectly the sure knowledge he draws from his religious faith and that such knowledge must be a confirmation and not a justification of any legislation at the civil level. In concrete terms, this might be translated thus: I am opposed to abortion, direct or indirect, not because I am a Catholic and my faith forbids it, but simply because such a practice goes directly against natural law which forbids the murder of an innocent. It can easily be seen from the way this is said that my position does not rest fundamentally on my religious faith but rather on natural law. My faith only confirms my opinion.
Here is another example. It seems to me that we should extend the scope of the divorce law. Instead of only one ground, four or five others could warrant the dissolution of a marriage. I am a Catholic and I do not approve of divorce, except in the specific cases determined by the church. But if today I am taking such a position, I am not going against my religious convictions, but I am considering, in the first place, the common good of the country which includes a multiplicity of religions.
Now, I only have to discuss the means of preventing conception. I do not suggest, Mr. Speaker, that I am an expert on the various means, appliances, tablets or contraceptives invented by modern science; I do not have any inferiority complex and I feel all the more at ease to speak about this, because I know that medical science although it is well advanced, is still proceeding by trial and error.

Mr. Speaker, on rising to comment on this proposed bill of the hon. member tor Buma-by-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) I would like to ask in the first instance what else is new, when he quotes as an example the fact that the Department of National Defence is spending money on contraceptives although this is against the law of the land? I presume the former minister of national defence had to O.K. those expenditures, and I would point out that he used to sing in the choir of a large United Church in Toronto. I notice that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has been quoting some statements issued by the United Church of Canada in support of his stand on this matter. It is interesting to note that the former choirboy in the United Church in Toronto is following the policy of his church in this regard, even though it may break the law of the land.
The breaking of the law of the land by the Department of National Defence is a poor example to set as one that everybody else should follow. Really we except the cabinet, to set an example to all the people in the observance of the law of the land as passed by parliament. When the cabinet proceeds to kill the intent of the capital punishment statute by commuting every death sentence that is imposed, and then tells us in its self-righteousness that it is exercising the quality of mercy, and that this makes it possible for members of the cabinet to set aside the law of the land, do not forget that the cabinet can also quote the Bible to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond when they buy contraceptives against the law of the land by simply saying to him, "Don't let your right hand know what your left hand doeth". When the cabinet is following the injunction contained in the sermon on the mount I say it is very poor policy on the part of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond to let the right hand know what the left hand does, among the 25 members of the cabinet. If he had not brought that to the attention of the members of the cabinet they would have followed the biblical injunction, and the other members of the cabinet would not have known what the former choirboy had been doing in the past.

Also do not forget that under the Department of Public Works they were throwing illegal fill into lake Ontario despite the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act. But I am counting on seeing that act enforced in the future because, by order in council, its administration has been transferred from the Department of Public Works to the Department of Transport, and the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) happens to be the former minister of national defence. Now since he was buying contraceptives against the law of the land I can see that in his new position as Minister of Transport he may continue to kick the law of the land in the teeth, just to set an example to the people of this nation so that they can see how the cabinet observes the law of the land, so that if the public want to break the law of the land that will be O.K.
I must express sympathy to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond in that I have looked up the first occasion when second reading of this bill was called, and I regret to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the second reading of this bill first came on September 11,	1964. Here it is now
November 17, 1967, more than three years later. If this country wants a perfect example of the importance that the cabinet attaches to private members of parliament, this is it.
I admire the sincerity of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. I know that he has spent a lot of time and thought on this question and everything he says rings with sincerity, but to think that the cabinet of this nation, which controls the agenda of this parliament from day to day, should never make it possible for him to speak on such a subject in more than three years is a clear indication of the attention members of the cabinet want to pay to private members of parliament, and it is a clear indication of how little attention they do pay to private members of parliament.
I am not one who feels that because a private member of parliament is sitting in the opposition, absolutely no attention should be paid to him. the same way they treat the private members who sit to the right of the Speaker. I maintain that all members of parliament have the same equal rights and, foolish as it may seem, I feel that a private member when elected to this house should represent his people in the same manner as members of the cabinet represent the people who sent them down to this house.

That is what a free vote is. We are going to have another free vote on this question of contraceptives. I would suggest that the private member's bill that is being brought forward at this time, and pressed with such fervour by a very, very sincere man, be withdrawn, giving precedence to the bill which will be introduced from the government side of the house. Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill I should like to say that it has been with interest that I have found that the government intends to bring forward, or already has brought forward, a bill on this subject so that the situation we now have will be corrected. In order to be a good law,
November 17, 1967

Amendment Respecting Birth Control a law must be enforceable. The present situation is one in which sales are being made which are not legal. The explanatory notes state that this section of the Criminal Code makes it an offence to supply any information on the subject of birth control or family planning in Canada. Section 150 (3) of the Criminal Code states:
No person shall be convicted of an offence under this section if he establishes that the public good was served by the acts that are alleged to constitute the offence and that the acts alleged did not extend beyond what served the public good.
This section of the code has been tested in the courts. I believe in 1937 in the Ottawa area a lady who had been giving out family planning information carried on her defence under this section, and it was found that under the laws of Canada, taking that section into account, it is legal to supply such information.
The question of birth control or family planning is something which has been considered by civilizations, down through the years. When we look back quite a number of years ago we find that the methods perhaps were different then. The Greeks or the Romans had methods in their time. One was the wearing of amulets, the tooth of a child, glass from a marble quarry, part of a cat's liver or the womb of a lioness. These, of course, would be difficult to acquire today. In North Africa a Koranic formula was bound to the wrist. In many places precious stones were worn in rings. In the thirteenth century a Dominican friar, and doctor, Albert the Great, recommended that a woman spit three times into the mouth of a frog. When one considers how a frog moves around he can appreciate how difficult that would be. In Japan a pebble of jasper was held in the hand, or dead bees were eaten.

I mention these things to indicate that down through the years this has peen a subject of deep concern to all civilizations. The reason for family planning is perhaps twofold; first, on the basis of a whole world proposition and, second, in the way it affects the individual family unit. I would suggest that any legislation we pass on this or any similar matter should be geared to the family unit in order to strengthen it and ensure a better life for our people, if we can. In recent years we have sent food to other countries, the depressed areas of the world. This has not resulted in the desired objective of a better life. It has improved the health of people so that they can die from starvation instead of from disease. Nature itself has a way to take care of population. I should like to cover that further; but to get back to the question of the family life and the necessity that many parents control the size of their families, I believe this is a very real and important thing, and that there should be no legislation to prevent it.
When a husband and wife desire to contain the size of their family unit, in order to ensure that the child growing up has a better life, is better fed and clothed and has a real opportunity to gain a good education which is not curtailed because of a large family, I believe this is something which is desirable, and I believe also that we should do all we can to see that this result is obtained.
